source_text: XXV. Unde patet, ut agnoscit Strangius loco citato, λογομαχίαν meram esse inter eos qui affirmant omnes voluntatis actiones liberas esse, & inter eos qui liberas esse negant. Nam qui istud affirmant libertatem late sumunt pro libentia illa qua voluntas ultro sequitur judicium intellectus, quo sensu nemo est qui neget omnem omnino voluntatis actionem liberam esse. Qui autem istud negant, libertatem accipiunt pro illa per naturam indeterminatione, & indifferentia, quae voluntati competit respectu actuum illorum qui sub deliberationem & consultationem cadunt. Quo sensu manifestum est, & ab omnibus concessum voluntatem liberam non esse respectu quorundam ipsius actuum. Sed cum latior ista libertatis acceptio minus recepta sit atque usitata, quantum autem fieri potest cum pluribus loquendum sit, quando simpliciter loquimur, omnino convenit, ut potius negemus, quam affirmemus voluntatem liberam esse in iis actibus, circa quos priorem tantum, non vero posteriorem & stricte dictam libertatem exercet.
english: So it is clear, as Strang admits in the passage cited, that the dispute between those who say all the will's acts are free and those who deny it is merely a quarrel about words (logomachia).

Those who say so take freedom broadly, as the willingness with which the will readily follows the intellect's judgement; in that sense no one would deny that every act of the will without exception is free. Those who deny it take freedom as the openness and indifference by nature that the will has toward acts that come under weighing and deliberation. In that sense it is obvious, and everyone grants, that the will is not free with respect to some of its acts.

But the broader use of 'freedom' is less accepted and less common, and we should speak with the majority as far as we can. So when we speak without qualification, it is entirely proper to deny rather than affirm that the will is free in acts where it exercises only the first kind of freedom and not the second, strict kind.

source_text: XXVI. Praeterea videtur in eo justo timidior tertia sententia quod non audet libertatem actionum humanarum ab omni necessitate proprie dicta vindicare: ne scilicet, in eo quicquam praejudicetur decretorum divinorum immutabilitati, & efficaciae gratiae divinae, aut determinationi voluntatis per judicium rationis practicae. Nam ut providentiae & gratiae divinae sua constet efficacia, & decretis Divinis sua vis & immutabilitas, adeoque etiam sua menti in voluntatem jura, non necesse est liberum hominis arbitrium ulli proprie dictae necessitati subjicere, ut ostendunt viri inter Reformatos Doctissimi, & nos quoque cum illis, si Deus dederit, ostensuros speramus.
english: Further, the third opinion seems overly timid in not daring to claim that human actions are free from every necessity in the proper sense. Its fear, of course, is that this would take something away from the unchangeableness of God's decrees, the efficacy of his grace, or the will's being settled by the judgement of practical reason.

But to keep the efficacy of providence and divine grace, the force and unchangeableness of God's decrees, and the mind's rights over the will, there is no need to subject man's free choice to any necessity in the proper sense. The most learned men among the Reformed show this, and we hope, God willing, to show it with them.

source_text: XXVII. Itaque cum Amesio & Roberto Baronio dicere non veremur humani arbitrii libertatem opponi necessitati cuivis proprie dictae, nec ullum hominis actum, si stricte & proprie loquamur liberum esse, nisi ponamus in homine veram & intrinsecam potestatem aliter agendi, aut saltem actum suum suspendendi, & ab actione cessandi. Per necessitatem enim proprie dictam intelligimus illam, quae ad certam actionem sic agens determinat, ut in eo non maneat vera & intrinseca potestas non agendi, aut aliter agendi.
english: So, with Ames and Robert Baron, we are not afraid to say that the freedom of human choice is opposed to every necessity in the proper sense. Strictly and properly speaking, no human act is free unless we grant that man has a real, inward power to act otherwise, or at least to hold back his act and stop acting.
By necessity in the proper sense we mean what fixes the agent on a given action in such a way that no real, inward power remains in him not to act or to act otherwise.

source_text: XXVIII. Itaque libertas hominis in agendo non male constituitur in quadam ejus circa actus suos indeterminatione & indifferentia. Verum observandum est per istam indifferentiam non intelligi, ut quidam suspicari videntur, statum ancipitem hominis fluctuantis, necdum certi quo vergat atque inclinet; sed veram potestatem agendi, vel non agendi, & actionem suam sic, vel sic instituendi; quae manet etiam in eo, qui proprio judicio atque electione se ad actiones has, aut illas determinavit, & apud quem certum & constitutum est hoc & non aliud agere.
english: So it is not wrong to place man's freedom in acting in a certain openness and indifference he has toward his acts.

Note, however, that this indifference does not mean, as some seem to suppose, the uncertain state of a man who wavers and has not yet settled which way to turn and lean. It means a real power to act or not act, and to arrange his action one way or another. That power remains even in someone who by his own judgement and choice has settled on these actions or those, and for whom it is fixed and decided to do this and nothing else.

source_text: XXIX. Proinde vulgata illa definitio, juxta quam libertas humana in eo statuitur, quod positis omnibus ad agendum requisitis, homo possit agere, vel non agere, hoc aut illud agere, licet quidam ea abutantur, bonum tamen & commodum sensum habere potest. Nam in actionibus omnibus deliberatis, quae solae proprie & stricte liberae sunt, homo non solum antequam agat, sed etiam dum agit, habet veram & realem potentiam non agendi, aut aliter agendi. Non potest quidem homo agere duo opposita simul, aut simul & agere & ab actione cessare: Sed tamen quum hoc agit, manet in eo potestas ad actum oppositum, aut ad cessationem ab illa actione. Quod Scholastici dicunt in libero arbitrio esse simultatem potentiae ad opposita, sed non potentiam simultatis, id est, potentiam ad opposita simul habenda. Cujus rei ratio est, quia potentia ad unum actum non opponitur potentiae ad illius actus negationem aut ad actum contrarium; sed duo contraria, aut contradicentia non possunt esse simul in eodem subjecto.
english: The common definition places human freedom in a man's being able, when everything needed for acting is present, to act or not act, or to do this or that. Some misuse it, but it can bear a good and suitable sense.

In all deliberate actions, which alone are free in the proper and strict sense, a man has a true and real power not to act or to act otherwise, not only before he acts but while he is acting. He cannot, of course, do two opposite things at once, or act and stop acting at the same time. Yet while he does the one, the power for the opposite act, or for stopping, remains in him.

The schoolmen express this by saying that free choice has a simultaneity of power for opposites, but not a power of simultaneity, that is, a power to have the opposites at once. The reason is that a power for one act is not opposed to a power for not doing it or for doing the contrary, whereas two contraries or contradictories cannot be in the same subject at once.

source_text: XXX. Praeter authores quartae sententiae, id agnoscit Joannes Strangius in libro illo tertio jam citato cap. 15. Quanquam enim neget hanc esse definitionem libertatis in genere, fatetur tamen illam convenire libero arbitrio strictius sumpto, prout non obstantibus praerequisitis ad agendum, superest ei indifferentia activa per quam immunis est ab omni necessitate antecedente, sive ea proveniat a praedeterminatione divina, sive a natura ipsius voluntatis, & certa objecti conditione. pag. 698. Strictior autem ista libertatis acceptio maxime usitata est, & propterea censeri debet maxime propria. Rem autem istam sic explicat pag. 696. In rebus, inquit, ad finem spectantibus, aut in rebus adiaphoris, in quibus non est necesse ut intellectus judicet ea habere necessariam connexionem cum bono in communi, verum est in sensu diviso, cum de actionibus elicitis, tum Imperatis, quod voluntas non tantum positis omnibus ad actionem praerequisitis, sed etiam cum voluntas determinata est, sive a Deo, sive, a seipsa ad agendum, & cum agit, retinet potentiam ad agendum hoc, aut illud, vel ad agendum aut non agendum. Ac proinde in ejusmodi rebus voluntas, non tantum antequam determinatur & agit, sed etiam cum determinatur & agit, manet libera, & omnino libere agit, quia etiam cum agit, retinet facultatem qua possit non agere, licet ex hypothesi quod determinetur aut agat, fieri non possit ut non agat; quia quicquid est, supposito quod sit, necessario est, licet simpliciter sit res contingens. Posita itaque determinatione divina, sive per gratiam efficacem, sive quacunque alia ratione, infertur quidem necessitas consequentiae, quod infallibiliter sequatur ille actus voluntatis ad quem determinata est a Deo, sed non est necessitas consequentis, quod sua natura manet contingens.
english: Besides the authors of the fourth opinion, John Strang admits this in the same third book, chapter 15. He denies that this is the definition of freedom in general, but grants that it fits free choice in the stricter sense, in that, whatever the prerequisites for acting, free choice keeps an active indifference that frees it from all antecedent necessity, whether that comes from divine predetermination or from the nature of the will itself and some particular state of the object (p. 698). And this stricter use of 'freedom' is the most common, and should therefore be counted the most proper.

He explains the matter this way (p. 696): "In things that concern the end, or in matters indifferent, where the intellect need not judge that they are necessarily connected with the good in general, it is true in the divided sense, of elicited and of commanded actions alike, that the will keeps the power to do this or that, or to act or not act. It keeps it not only when everything prerequisite to action is present, but also when it has been settled to act, whether by God or by itself, and while it is acting.

"In such things, then, the will stays free, and acts altogether freely, not only before it is settled and acts but also when it is settled and acts. Even while acting it keeps the faculty by which it could refrain, although on the hypothesis that it is settled or acting it cannot fail to act. Whatever is, given that it is, is necessarily, though taken simply it is a contingent thing.

"So once divine determination is granted, whether by efficacious grace or in any other way, there follows a necessity of the consequence, namely that the act of the will to which God has settled it follows infallibly. But there is no necessity of the consequent, because the act remains contingent by its nature."

source_text: XXXI. Non improbat quoque Andreas Rivetus ut liberum arbitrium dicatur talis facultas voluntatis, qua positis omnibus ad agendum praerequisitis, possit agere, aut non agere. Modo id intelligatur non in sensu composito sed in sensu diviso. Nempe, si quis dicat, positis omnibus antecedentibus requisitis, secundum ordinem rationis, vel temporis ad actum, liberum arbitrium posse operari, vel non operari, ita videlicet, ut cum eisdem praerequisitis stet simul in libero arbitrio facultas, & potentia, qua possit operari, vel non operari si velit, ut distinguit Didacus Alvares, quia etiam motio Dei efficax qua ad talem actum voluntas determinatur, non tollit a libero arbitrio facultatem operandi illum actum, vel operandi actum contrarium, sed solum efficit, quod cum liberum arbitrium possit operari, & non operari talem actum, infallibiliter, libere tamen, operetur illum. Quae sunt verba viri illius Doctissimi summae controversiarum tract. 4. quaest. 3. Quibus addit liberum arbitrium creatum, non solum antequam determinetur ad unum actum, sed etiam in ipso instanti, in quo determinatur a Deo, & seipsum determinat ad eundem actum, simul habere potentiam, qua potest actum contrarium producere si velit, non tamen ad actum contrarium simul habendum, quia duo actus contrarii simul in eadem potentia esse non possunt, sed successive.
english: Andrew Rivet, too, does not object to calling free choice the faculty of the will by which, when everything prerequisite for acting is present, it can act or not act, provided this is taken in the divided sense and not the composite.

His words, in the Summary of Controversies (treatise 4, question 3), are: "That is, if one says that when all the antecedent requisites for the act are present, in order of reason or of time, free choice can act or not act, meaning that together with those same prerequisites there is in free choice the faculty and power by which it can act or not act if it wills, as Diego Alvarez distinguishes. For even God's efficacious motion, by which the will is settled on such an act, does not take from free choice the faculty to do that act or the contrary one. It only brings it about that free choice, though able to do or not do such an act, does it infallibly, yet freely."

He adds that created free choice, not only before it is settled on one act but at the very instant in which God settles it and it settles itself on that act, has at the same time the power by which it can produce the contrary act if it wills. It does not, however, have a power to have the contrary act at the same time, because two contrary acts cannot be in one power at once, only one after the other.

source_text: XXXII. Praesertim vero Ludovicus Crocius dum viveret in Schola Bremensi Theologiae Doctor & Professor, hanc & non aliam libertatis definitionem tradit, Libertas humanae voluntatis, est ejus naturalis proprietas, qua ab intellectu, aut sensu sub ratione boni sibi proposita eligere, & positis omnibus ad agendum requisitis, actionem suscipere velle, aut suspendere potest. In Theol. Syntag. lib. 3. cap. 37. thes. 3. Ubi subjungit liberum arbitrium eodem sensu a Patribus antiquis dictum esse. Ut & in ejusdem Theseos explicatione notat libertatem quae voluntatis proprietas naturalis est, opponi necessitati, sive illa sit a causa externa cogente, sive a natura intrinsecus ad unum absolute determinante.
english: Ludwig Crocius in particular, while he lived doctor and professor of theology at the School of Bremen, gives this definition of freedom and no other: "The freedom of the human will is its natural property by which it can choose what the intellect or sense sets before it under the aspect of good, and, when everything needed for acting is present, can will to take up an action or to hold it back." (Theological Syntagma, book 3, chapter 37, thesis 3.)

He adds there that the ancient Fathers spoke of free choice in the same sense. And in explaining the same thesis he notes that freedom, the will's natural property, is opposed to necessity, whether it comes from an outside cause that compels or from nature fixing the will inwardly and absolutely on one outcome.

source_text: XXXIII. Caeterum quando libertas constituitur in quadam agendi indifferentia, & in eo quod qui liber dicitur potest agere, vel non agere, hoc, aut illud agere, sedulo animadvertendum est quod istud ita accipi non debet, quasi ad essentiam libertatis pertineret, ut qui liber est possit bene, vel male agere. Nam posse male agere non est aliquid quod ad libertatis perfectionem pertineat, sed potius quaedam est imperfectio libertatem comitans in persona creata, & quae libertati accidentaria est. Nam Deus qui est omnium in agendo liberrimus male agere non potest: ut nec possunt sancti Angeli ex quo fuerunt a Deo in gratia confirmati. Et haec quoque praerogativa est Animarum Beatarum, quae ad Dei Visionem semel admissae fuerunt, ut amplius peccare non possint. Neque tamen propterea vel sancti Angeli, vel animae Beatae libertatem suam amiserunt.
english: When freedom is placed in a certain indifference of acting, in the free agent's being able to act or not act, to do this or that, we must take great care not to read this as if it belonged to the essence of freedom that the free agent can do either good or evil.

Being able to do evil is no part of freedom's perfection. It is rather an imperfection that goes along with freedom in a created person, something accidental to it. God, the freest of all agents, cannot do evil. Neither can the holy angels, from the time God confirmed them in grace.
This is also the privilege of the blessed souls once admitted to the vision of God: they can never sin again. Yet that does not mean the holy angels or the blessed souls have lost their freedom.

source_text: XXXIV. Et ex adverso posse bene agere, & operari quae Deo grata sint & placeant, perfectio quaedam est, quae potest abesse ab agente libero, salva manente libertatis natura atque essentia. Quippe omnium consensu libertas in agendo mansit in daemonibus & angelis tenebrarum, nec prorsus illa perit in hominibus aeternae damnationi a Deo addictis; & tamen nec Diabolus, nec homines damnati bene agere possunt & aliquid facere quod a Deo probetur. Imo neque in hac vita homo per peccatum corruptus, & gratia Dei destitutus, quicquam praestare valet quod revera sit bonum & Deo placens. Juxta illud Domini nostri, Sine me nihil potestis facere, & consentaneum Apostoli dictum, Non quod sufficientes simus cogitare aliquid a nobis, quasi ex nobis: sed sufficientia nostra ex Deo est. Et nihilominus homo induratus, & plane a Deo desertus suam in agendo libertatem retinet. Joan. 15. ver. 5. 2 Cor. 3. ver. 5.
english: On the other hand, being able to do good and to do what is acceptable and pleasing to God is a perfection that a free agent can lack while the nature and essence of freedom stay intact.

Everyone agrees that freedom in acting has remained in the demons, the angels of darkness, and that it does not wholly perish in men whom God has given over to eternal damnation. Yet neither the devil nor the damned can do good or do anything God approves.

Indeed, even in this life man corrupted by sin and lacking God's grace cannot achieve anything truly good and pleasing to God. As our Lord says, "Without me you can do nothing" (John 15:5), and the Apostle agrees: "Not that we are sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as from ourselves; our sufficiency is from God" (2 Corinthians 3:5). And still a man who is hardened and plainly abandoned by God keeps his freedom in acting.

source_text: XXXV. Repugnat quidem divinae bonitati, justitiae, & sapientiae, ut formet creaturam aliquam intelligentem, sive rationalem, adeoque liberam, quae bene agere non possit, & quae necessitatem aliquam male agendi a Deo ipsam inditam habeat. Nec enim Deus Opt. Max. quicquam creare potest quod bonum non sit. Sed creatura quae bona a Deo producta fuit, culpa & vitio suo potest fieri mala, & eos male agendo contrahere habitus quibus ad malum ita determinetur, ut amplius bene agere non possit; voluntate, scilicet, in malo obdurata, nec valente, nisi gratiae divinae auxilio, sese ex iis laqueis extricare in quos sese ultro induit.
english: It does clash with God's goodness, justice and wisdom for him to form an intelligent or rational, and therefore free, creature that cannot do good and has some necessity of doing evil placed in it by God himself. God, supremely good and great, cannot create anything that is not good.

But a creature that God made good can become evil by its own fault and vice. By doing evil it can acquire habits that fix it on evil so firmly that it can no longer do good. Its will is then hardened in evil and cannot, without the help of divine grace, free itself from the snares it has willingly walked into.

source_text: XXXVI. Neque tamen creatura, quae propria culpa in hanc male agendi necessitatem conjecta est, in iis quae male agit, propterea libere non agit. Nec enim pravi habitus, quibus mens & voluntas ejus est praepedita, obstant quominus de iis quae agit consultet atque deliberet, & quin voluntas ultro, absque ulla vi cogente, rationis pravae, judicium sequatur. Imo ille ipse qui bene agere non potest, potest tamen a singulis malis actibus abstinere, nec ulla necessitate ad hoc, aut illud peccatum patrandum constringitur. Verbi causa, quum Diabolus tentationibus suis aliquem movet atque sollicitat, ut Deo rebellet & carni obsequatur, posset illum non tentare; & quum homo quispiam justo Dei judicio occaecatus atque induratus, flagitium aliquod admittit, ut caedem, aut adulterium, posset adulterio & caede illa se non polluere, nec ullam in eo potest praetexere necessitatem.
english: Yet a creature that its own fault has thrown into this necessity of doing evil does not on that account act unfreely in the evil it does. The corrupt habits that hamper its mind and will do not stop it from weighing and deliberating about what it does, nor stop its will from following the judgement of corrupt reason willingly, with no force compelling it.

In fact, one who cannot do good can still refrain from each particular evil act, and no necessity binds him to commit this sin or that. When the devil stirs and urges someone with temptations to rebel against God and obey the flesh, he could have left him untempted. When a man blinded and hardened by God's just judgement commits some crime, such as murder or adultery, he could have kept himself clean of that adultery and that murder, and he cannot plead any necessity for it.

source_text: XXXVII. Porro sic exposita libertatis humanae natura atque essentia, quaerendum superest ad quam hominis facultatem proprie spectet atque pertineat. Doctorum Scholae Reformatae communior sententia est libertatem humanam originem quidem a mente & ratione ducere, sed tamen esse proprie voluntatis affectionem. Quod enim homo inter varia eligere potest, & hoc nunc amplecti, alias rejicere, inde est quod de rebus varie judicare potest, & diversas boni, malive rationes in iis apprehendere: sed tamen nullus actus liber in homine censetur, nisi qui a voluntate, vel elicitur, vel saltem imperatur. Adeoque soli voluntatis actus per se liberi esse existimantur: qui vero per facultates alias exercentur, eatenus tantum liberi sunt, quatenus a voluntate pendent, & ea vel consentiente, vel saltem negligente, & connivente fiunt. Et hoc est quod Scholae dicunt libertatem esse formaliter in sola voluntate, in intellectu vero tantum radicaliter. Sic statuit hac de re Ludovicus Crocius loco supra citato. Libertas, inquit, quae arbitrio tribuitur, proprie est affectio voluntatis, quamvis radicem suam in intellectu & ratione habeat.
english: Having set out the nature and essence of human freedom in this way, we still have to ask which of man's faculties it properly concerns and belongs to.

The more common view among the teachers of the Reformed school is that human freedom has its origin in mind and reason but is properly a disposition of the will. Man can choose among various things, embracing one now and rejecting it at another time, because he can judge things in various ways and grasp in them different aspects of good or evil. Even so, no act in man counts as free unless the will either produces it or at least commands it.

So only the will's acts are held to be free in themselves. Acts carried out through other faculties are free only to the extent that they depend on the will and happen with its consent, or at least its neglect and toleration. That is what the schools mean by saying that freedom is formally in the will alone, and in the intellect only as in its root.
Ludwig Crocius settles the matter so in the passage cited above: "The freedom ascribed to choice is properly a disposition of the will, though it has its root in the intellect and reason."

source_text: XXXVIII. Quidam tamen inter Reformatos aliter ea de re Philosophantur. De quorum numero est Vir Clarissimus Moses Amyraldus. Ille ergo, ut mentem suam in hac quaestione explicet, observat libertatem tribus actuum generibus tribui. Et 1. quidem actibus earum facultatum quibus imperat voluntas. 2. Actibus voluntatis ipsius. 3. Actibus intellectus. Primo respectu, ex ejus sententia, libertas non est aliud quam facultas vivendi, seu agendi ut velis. Eatenus enim liberi censemur, quum nullo cogente, vel impediente, facimus id quod volumus. Secundo respectu libertas ab ipso definitur, Facultas volendi ut judicamus esse volendum, & ut quisque proprio judicio determinatur ad id, non alieno. Nam quemadmodum actiones corporeae censentur esse liberae, quia pendent ex principio libero, nempe voluntate, sic actiones voluntatis liberas esse dicit, quia pendent itidem ex principio libero, nempe, ex arbitrio intellectus. Libertatem autem intellectus sitam esse dicit in ejus αὐτοπραγίᾳ, id est, in eo quod intellectus ex se, & per se agit, estque αὐτεξούσιος, id est, potens suarum ipsius operationum, quia, scilicet, ad eas exercendas neque vi cogitur, neque ex alieno imperio pendet: adeo ut libertas, respectu actionum mentis & intellectus sit potestas judicandi de rebus αὐτεξούσιος, & quae neque a vi externa, neque ab externo imperio est. Quae latius exponit Vir ille Doctissimus libello de libero arbitrio Sect. 1. pag. 20. & seqq.
english: Some of the Reformed, however, reason differently about this. Among them is the distinguished Moses Amyraut. To explain his view on the question, he notes that freedom is ascribed to three kinds of acts: first, the acts of the faculties the will commands; second, the acts of the will itself; third, the acts of the intellect.

In the first respect, on his view, freedom is nothing but the ability to live or act as you will, for we count as free when, with nothing forcing or blocking us, we do what we want. In the second respect he defines freedom as "the ability to will as we judge should be willed, each person being settled on it by his own judgement and not another's." Bodily actions are counted free because they depend on a free source, the will; in the same way, he says, the will's actions are free because they too depend on a free source, the judgement of the intellect.

The intellect's freedom he places in its autopragia: the intellect acts from itself and through itself, and is autexousios, in control of its own operations, since it is neither forced by violence to perform them nor dependent on anyone else's command. So freedom, with respect to the acts of the mind and intellect, is a self-governing power of judging about things that comes neither from outside force nor from outside command. That learned man develops this more fully in his short book On Free Choice, section 1, p. 20 and following.

source_text: XXXIX. Ex qua doctrina sequitur libertatem illam quae in actionibus externis reperitur, in iis dependenter esse a voluntate: eam vero quae convenit actibus voluntatis, in illis dependenter esse ab intellectu, intellectum vero esse per se liberum, adeoque libertatem primario & praecipue intellectui competere, & in eo esse reponendam, tanquam in propria & naturali sede: ac proinde libertatem non esse formaliter, ut multis placet, in sola voluntate; in intellectu vero tantum causaliter & radicaliter, sicuti docet, & probare contendit idem ille Vir Doctissimus libelli sui pag. 30. & sequentibus: Et praecipue quidem hoc argumento, quod ejus judicio, intellectus naturaliter magis est sui juris quam voluntas; quoniam voluntas intellectus ductum sequitur, ac ejus veluti gubernationi subjecta est, qua de causa a Graecis appellatur τὸ ἡγεμονικόν. Absurdum autem putat, in ea potius facultate libertatem esse formaliter, quae alieno imperio subest, quam in ea quae nullius alius facultatis legibus obstricta tenetur.
english: From this teaching it follows that the freedom found in outward actions depends in them on the will, while the freedom that belongs to the will's acts depends in them on the intellect. The intellect, however, is free in itself. So freedom belongs first and chiefly to the intellect and should be placed there as in its own natural seat.

Hence freedom is not, as many would have it, formally in the will alone while being in the intellect only as its cause and root. The same learned man teaches this and tries to prove it on p. 30 and following of his short book.

His main argument is that in his judgement the intellect is by nature more its own master than the will. The will follows the intellect's lead and is subject, as it were, to its rule, which is why the Greeks call the intellect to hegemonikon, the governing part. He thinks it absurd that freedom should be formally in the faculty under another's command rather than in the one bound by the laws of no other faculty.

source_text: XL. Et tamen in ejusdem sectionis fine concludit libertatem, proprie loquendo, non esse formaliter, vel in intellectu, vel in voluntate, si seorsim considerentur, sed in utraque facultate conjunctim. Quia, scilicet, homo liber esse non censetur, neque simpliciter quatenus judicat, nec simpliciter quatenus appetit, sed quatenus appetit ex judicio atque consilio rationis. Quemadmodum humanitas neque formaliter est in anima intelligente, neque formaliter in sola natura sensitiva, sed in homine quatenus ex duabus illis naturis componitur. Ac proinde, juxta illius sententiam, liberum arbitrium non est una quaepiam e facultatibus rationalibus quae in homine sunt; nec etiam quicquam tale cujus una pars potius ad intellectum, altera potius ad voluntatem pertineat: sed est utriusque facultatis, intellectus, scilicet, ac voluntatis, ea indoles atque affectio, secundum quam concurrentes, quaeque pro ingenio suo, ad actiones hominis, fit ut homo, quatenus homo est, liber esse censeatur. Quanquam, quemadmodum in definitione hominis, rationis quam naturae animalis consideratio longe magis excellit, sic in definitione liberi arbitrii, intellectus quam appetitus ratio longe potior esse videtur. Convenit enim multis aliis rebus ut appetant, unus homo inter creaturas aspectabiles, quia solus est praeditus intellectu, libere appetere putatur.
english: Yet at the end of the same section he concludes that freedom, properly speaking, is not formally in the intellect or in the will taken separately, but in both faculties together. Man is not counted free simply in that he judges, nor simply in that he desires, but in that he desires on the judgement and counsel of reason. In the same way humanity is not formally in the understanding soul, nor in the sensitive nature alone, but in man as made up of those two natures.

On his view, then, free choice is not any one of the rational faculties in man, nor something with one part belonging more to the intellect and another more to the will. It is the character and disposition of both faculties, intellect and will, by which, as they work together on human actions, each in its own way, man as man is counted free.

Still, just as in defining man the element of reason counts far more than that of animal nature, so in defining free choice the intellect seems to weigh far more than appetite. Many other things desire, but among visible creatures man alone is thought to desire freely, because he alone has an intellect.

source_text: XLI. Intellectum autem quovis modo consideratum non vult esse principium libertatis in homine, sed tantum quatenus de rebus agendis, aut appetendis pronunciat: neque id solum in genere, sed etiam in singulari; & ita ut hominem ad agendum impellat, aut ab actione retrahat: quo respectu vocatur intellectus practicus: qui, scilicet, dictat in rebus singulis, quid jam, hic & nunc agendum, aut non agendum, appetendum, aut fugiendum sit. Nec tamen adhuc ad libere agendum, judicium quodvis intellectus practici sufficere existimat: sed requirit judicium tale quod sit conclusio consultationis, & deliberationis. Adeo ut, ex ejus mente, intellectus practicus quovis modo & simpliciter in homine non sit principium actionum liberarum; sed tantum quatenus de rebus agendis judicat προβουλεύτως, id est, habita prius deliberatione, & consultatione: sicuti videre est sect. citata pag. 31. & seqq.
english: He does not, however, make the intellect the source of freedom in man however it is taken, but only in so far as it pronounces on what is to be done or desired, not only in general but in the particular case, and so as to drive a man to act or hold him back from acting. In that respect it is called the practical intellect, which dictates in each particular matter what is to be done or not done, sought or shunned, here and now.

Even then he does not think any judgement of the practical intellect is enough for free action. He requires a judgement that is the conclusion of weighing and deliberation. On his view, then, the practical intellect is not the source of free actions in man in just any way, but only when it judges what to do probouleutos, that is, after deliberation and weighing have taken place. This can be seen in the section cited, p. 31 and following.

source_text: XLII. Porro Josue Placeus vir quoque Doctissimus, Amyraldi dum viveret Collega, istud habet cum eo commune, quod existimat libertatem non esse formaliter in sola voluntate; nec solam voluntatem sed etiam intellectum esse facultatem liberam; verum in eo differt a Collega, quod alter ille distinguit inter libertatem quae competit intellectui, & libertatem quae competit voluntati, & utrique suam peculiarem definitionem assignat; hic vero vult illam eandem libertatem, a qua voluntas libera nominatur, intellectui quoque convenire: Etenim libertas illa, ex ejus mente, sita est in immunitate a triplici necessitate, coactionis nempe, determinationis a materia, & determinationis a sensu. Quae immunitas ut ipse arbitratur, ad intellectum ex aequo pertinet. Ac praeterea in eo sententia illius priori opposita est, quod si voluntas & intellectus inter se conferantur, libertas penes voluntatem ipsi magis esse videtur. Idque quia censet imperium & dominium in homine esse potius penes voluntatem, quam penes intellectum: propterea quod intellectus voluntatem non movet per suum actum veluti per imperium, sed per objectum quod ipsi proponit; voluntas autem mentem movet, & applicat ad intelligendum per suum actum, tanquam per imperium. Quicquid sit tamen putat ille Vir Doctus quosdam mentis nostrae actus liberos esse, adeoque bonos, aut malos moraliter, qui tamen ex voluntatis imperio non fiunt, nec ab ejus consensu, ut a sui quodam principio pendent, cujusmodi actus censet esse fidem & haeresin illi oppositam. Ut videre est in ejus Opusculis Posthumis tract. de lib. Arbitr. pag. 163. & 164.
english: Josué de la Place, another very learned man and Amyraut's colleague while he lived, agrees with him that freedom is not formally in the will alone, and that the intellect as well as the will is a free faculty.

He differs from his colleague in this: Amyraut distinguishes the freedom that belongs to the intellect from the freedom that belongs to the will and gives each its own definition, whereas de la Place holds that the very freedom by which the will is called free also belongs to the intellect. On his view that freedom lies in exemption from three necessities: compulsion, being settled by matter, and being settled by sense. And that exemption, he judges, belongs to the intellect just as much.

His view is also opposed to Amyraut's in this: when will and intellect are compared, he thinks freedom lies more with the will. The reason is that he thinks command and mastery in man rest with the will rather than the intellect. The intellect does not move the will by its act as by a command, but by the object it sets before it; the will, by contrast, moves the mind and applies it to understanding by its act, as by a command.

Even so, that learned man thinks that some acts of our mind are free, and so morally good or evil, though they are not done at the will's command and do not depend on its consent as on their source. He counts faith, and the heresy opposed to it, among such acts. See his Posthumous Works, treatise On Free Choice, pp. 163-164.

source_text: XLIII. Celeberrimus autem jam dictus Alexander Morus, cum Viris illis Doctis, censet intellectum atque voluntatem liberum arbitrium inter se veluti partiri: & liberum arbitrium non esse aliud quam intellectum atque voluntatem, quatenus hae duae facultates concurrunt, & quodam quasi vinculo, sive conjugio inter se continentur. In utra vero potius facultate consistat, in medio relinquit. Sicut enim, inquit, arbitrium intellectus terminatur in voluntate, ita libertas voluntatis radicem habet in intellectu. Adeo ut, ex ejus mente, liberum arbitrium dici possit intellectus quatenus voluntatem movet atque afficit: vel voluntas quatenus ab intellectu movetur. Sive ipsius Aristotelis verbis ἢ ὀρεκτικὸς νοῦς, ἢ ὄρεξις διανοητική. De Gratia & libero arbitrio disp. 1. thes. 21.
english: Alexander More, the famous man already mentioned, holds with those learned men that intellect and will in a sense divide free choice between them. Free choice, he thinks, is nothing but intellect and will in so far as the two faculties work together and are held together by a kind of bond or marriage. Which of the two faculties it rests in more, he leaves open.

"For as the choice of the intellect ends in the will," he says, "so the freedom of the will has its root in the intellect." On his view, then, free choice can be called the intellect as it moves and affects the will, or the will as the intellect moves it. In Aristotle's own words, it is "either desiring mind or thinking desire" (On Grace and Free Choice, disputation 1, thesis 21).

source_text: XLIV. Quantum ad me attinet, existimo nullum actum ullius facultatis, etiam mentis ipsius in homine, liberum esse, nisi qui a voluntate quodammodo pendeat, & ea vel imperante, vel aliquomodo consentiente fiat; adeoque ut clarius dicam, quem homo non potuisset omittere, si voluisset. Quis enim ab homine libere actum dicat, quod ab homine, etsi maxime voluerit, non potuit aliter fieri; & ad quod nullomodo directe, vel indirecte, mediate, vel immediate, supponitur illius concurrisse voluntas? Ac cum omnis actio libera sub praeceptum cadere possit, & virtutis, vel vitii rationem induere, necesse est ut a voluntate quodammodo procedat. Hactenus enim in Scholis communi consensu recepta est Augustini sententia, peccatum non habere rationem peccati, si non sit voluntarium, id est, si voluntas ejus aliqua ratione principium & causa non sit, prout communis fidelium sensus dictum illud interpretatur.
english: For my part, I think no act of any faculty in man, not even of the mind itself, is free unless it depends in some way on the will and happens either at its command or with some kind of its consent. To put it more plainly: unless it is an act the man could have left undone if he had wished.

Who would call an act freely done by a man if he could not have made it otherwise however much he wanted to, and if his will is not supposed to have taken part in it in any way, directly or indirectly, mediately or immediately?

Again, since every free action can fall under a command and take on the character of virtue or vice, it must come in some way from the will. That is why the schools have so far agreed in accepting Augustine's maxim that sin is not sin unless it is voluntary, that is, unless the sinner's will is in some way its source and cause, which is how the common understanding of the faithful takes that saying.

source_text: XLV. Neque tamen inde consequens est, ut libertas dicatur esse formaliter in sola voluntate. Etenim quemadmodum omnis actio libera ortum suum voluntati aliquomodo debet, sic quoque omnis actio libera nascitur ex aliqua mentis consultatione, & deliberatione. Et sicut intellectus nullam actionem libere elicit quam non potuerit impedire voluntas, ita quoque nullus actus voluntatis liber est, de quo non licuerit menti consultare, atque deliberare. Unde sequitur aequo jure, ad mentem atque voluntatem referendas esse actiones liberas, ac proinde, si inde colligitur libertatem formaliter esse in voluntate, inde quoque colligi posse, illam formaliter esse in intellectu.
english: It does not follow, though, that freedom should be said to be formally in the will alone. Every free action owes its origin in some way to the will, but every free action also arises from some weighing and deliberation by the mind.

The intellect produces no action freely that the will could not have prevented, and in the same way no act of the will is free unless the mind was able to weigh and deliberate about it. With equal right, then, free actions must be traced to both mind and will. If one concludes from the first point that freedom is formally in the will, one can conclude from the second that it is formally in the intellect.

source_text: XLVI. Sed mihi potius dicendum videtur neque in intellectu, neque in voluntate libertatem esse formaliter, sed in homine quatenus per intellectum & voluntatem agit. Siquidem libertas proprie loquendo, non est affectio hujus, aut illius facultatis, sed aliquid oriens ex plurium facultatum relatione mutua & concursu; & quod proinde nulli certae facultati proprie attribui potest, sed solum supposito in quo facultates illae reperiuntur. Itaque si exacte loquamur, nec mens, nec voluntas liberae dicendae sunt, sed homo ipse quatenus facultatibus illis certo modo utitur. Quum vero voluntas libera vocatur, enunciatio non est, ut Scholae loquuntur, formalis, sed causalis: quia, scilicet, voluntas intellectui juncta, causa est actionum, quarum respectu homo libere agere dicitur. Quae observatio non est omnino de nihilo, ut in sequentibus videri poterit. Facit enim ad solvendas quasdam difficultates quibus se implicant non pauci, dum totam libertatis rationem in voluntate, non simpliciter in homine quaerunt.
english: My own view is rather that freedom is formally neither in the intellect nor in the will, but in man as he acts through intellect and will. Freedom, properly speaking, is not a disposition of this faculty or that. It arises from the mutual relation and joint working of several faculties, and so it cannot properly be ascribed to any one faculty, only to the subject (suppositum) in which those faculties are found.

Strictly speaking, then, neither mind nor will should be called free, but man himself, in so far as he uses those faculties in a certain way. When the will is called free, the statement is not, in the language of the schools, formal but causal: the will, joined to the intellect, is the cause of the actions for which man is said to act freely.

This point is not idle, as will appear later. It helps to resolve certain difficulties in which a good many entangle themselves by looking for the whole nature of freedom in the will rather than in the man as such.

source_text: XLVII. An autem ad libertatem hominis plus conferat intellectus quam voluntas, aut voluntas plusquam intellectus, res est quam definire Theologi non interest, & cujus accuratiorem inquisitionem neglexit ipse hodiernorum Philosophorum Princeps Aristoteles, ac propterea nos illam cum doctissimis quibusdam Theologis in medio quoque relinquimus.
english: Whether the intellect contributes more to man's freedom than the will, or the will more than the intellect, is not something the theologian needs to settle. Aristotle himself, the prince of today's philosophers, did not inquire into it closely.
So we too, along with some very learned theologians, leave the question open.

source_text: XLVIII. Caeterum utcunque inter se varient Scholae Reformatae Doctores, in explicando quae sit natura libertatis, & quibus facultatibus conveniat, aut non conveniat; nihilominus facile admittunt definitionem liberi Arbitrii quae traditur a Bellarmino, De Gratia & libero Arbitrio lib. 3. cap. 3. Nempe quod Liberum Arbitrium est libera potestas ex his quae ad finem aliquem conducunt unum prae alio eligendi, aut unum & idem respuendi, vel acceptandi, pro arbitrio nostro, intelligenti naturae, ad magnam Dei gloriam attributa, vel concessa. Id videre est apud Rob. Baronium in Metaphysica sua generali, sect. 12. Disp. de Libertate Arbitrii, ubi hanc definitionem non solum probat, sed etiam per partes accurate explicat. Eandem quoque definitionem non improbat Paraeus, quandoquidem quibusdam in eam animadversis, fatetur de libero Arbitrio absolute considerato, inter nos & Bellarminum nullam esse controversiam in locum jam dictum Bellarmini scribens. Neque multum discrepat a Bellarminiana definitio illa, quam tanquam planiorem, & pleniorem illi substituit; videlicet quod sit potentia volendi, nolendi, eligendi, repudiandi objectum ab intellectu monstratum, sine coactione, spontaneo ac deliberato motu, & aptitudine voluntatis ad volendum, aut nolendum opposita. Et similiter Amesius fatetur istam definitionem illum sensum habere posse, ut de ea non sit contendendi causa. in Bell. enerv. tom. 4. lib. 4. cap. 1.
english: However the teachers of the Reformed school differ in explaining the nature of freedom and the faculties it does or does not belong to, they readily accept Bellarmine's definition of free choice in On Grace and Free Choice (book 3, chapter 3): "Free choice is the free power, given or granted to an intelligent nature for the great glory of God, of choosing among things that lead to some end one rather than another, or of rejecting or accepting one and the same thing, as we judge fit."

Robert Baron shows this in his General Metaphysics (section 12, disputation On Freedom of Choice), where he not only approves the definition but explains it carefully part by part. Pareus does not reject it either. Commenting on that passage of Bellarmine, he makes some remarks on the definition and then admits that, on free choice considered absolutely, there is no dispute between us and Bellarmine.

The definition Pareus puts in its place as plainer and fuller is not far from Bellarmine's: free choice is "the power of willing, not willing, choosing or rejecting an object the intellect sets before it, without compulsion, by a spontaneous and deliberate movement, with the will able to will or not will the opposite." Likewise Ames grants that the definition can bear a sense that leaves no reason to quarrel over it (Bellarmine Disarmed, volume 4, book 4, chapter 1).
